title: The breath is the goddess moving
hook: a verse that sees the goddess herself rising and falling in every breath
carry: the breath is Shakti, rising and falling
tomorrow: when exactly does a bell stop ringing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vijnana Bhairava opened: the goddess asked for the real thing, and Bhairava gave doors instead of descriptions. Today, the first door. It's in your chest.

A swing at the playground hangs for a split second at the top of its arc, neither going nor coming. Every kid on one feels that hang in the stomach. A breath has the same moment, twice over, and it slips past all day, through meetings and traffic and sleep. Where in a breath is the easiest place to miss? The Vijnana Bhairava's first practice points straight at it, and says who is doing the turning.
screen: `THE SWING HANGS AT THE TOP.` → `A BREATH HAS THAT MOMENT.` → `THE TURN.`

segments.voice: Picture the scene. The goddess sits with Bhairava, Shiva in his fierce form, and asks him what he really is. He doesn't describe himself. He hands her doors. And the very first door he gives her is about her. In this verse the breath isn't just air. The supreme goddess herself, Bhairava says, rises as the breath going out, prana, and comes down as the breath coming in. Shakti, moving, every few seconds, in an ordinary chest. Then the instruction. Rest the attention at the two places where each breath begins, the turns, and the verse promises a state of fullness. Here's the big idea under it, and it runs through this whole tantric path: Shiva is the awareness, Shakti is the movement, and the two are never apart. Many teachers read the verse simply: you don't have to go anywhere to meet the goddess. She is already breathing. That's why the practice doesn't slow the breath, shape it or hold it. It leaves her movement alone, and turns the attention, the Shiva side, toward the place where she turns. The practices that follow stay close by, down to the still point between two breaths, a pause so small it usually passes without a name. In this text, that gap isn't empty. It's where the two meet. So on a night you can't sleep, the breath you're fighting isn't the enemy. In this tradition, it's the goddess, still moving. The real thing can't be described. But it can be noticed, as close as the next breath.
screen: `THE FIRST DOOR IS ABOUT HER.` · `SHE IS BREATH. REST AT THE TURNS.` · `SHIVA AWARENESS, SHAKTI MOVEMENT.` · `DON'T SHAPE IT. THE STILL POINT.` · then, large: `SHE IS ALREADY BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go on its own; don't shape it. If it helps, picture it the way the verse does: the goddess rising, the goddess coming down. Feel for the turn at the top, where the in-breath ends, and at the bottom, where the out-breath ends. Rest your attention there, lightly, and let it fill.
The Vijnana Bhairava: here, its first door, the breath as the goddess moving, and attention resting at its two turns.
For the road: the breath is Shakti, rising and falling. She is already breathing. Until tomorrow.

prana.meaning: the breath going out; also breath and life

apana.meaning: the breath coming in, in this practice

Bhairava.meaning: Shiva in his fierce form, the teacher in this book

Vijnana Bhairava.meaning: a short tantric book of doors for the attention

Shakti.meaning: the goddess as power and movement

sources.ref: Vijnana Bhairava, the first dharana (the supreme goddess, whose nature is visarga, rising as prana and descending as jiva/apana; fixing attention at the two points where each arises brings a state of fullness)
Vijnana Bhairava, the breath dharanas that follow (the voids at the two turns; the breath as Shakti neither going out nor coming in, in the middle)

notes: Vijnana Bhairava run, day 2. Confirm the first dharana (verse 24 in common numbering): prana rising/going out, jiva or apana coming in, attention fixed at the two points of their arising, with the state of Bhairava as the fruit; and the following verse on the pause between them.
The text's terms for out- and in-breath vary by verse and reading (prana/apana, prana/jiva); the lesson uses prana and apana as the familiar pair. Keeper to confirm.
'Some breathing practices work on the breath' is a soft contrast with general breath-control methods, not a claim about any tradition; cut if the Keeper prefers.
